t: Why is learning to read hard?
q: Yet, after one full year of schooling — 975 hours of teaching — and hours of support at home, Laura had still not learned to read.
She was quickly given extra reading lessons, and within a half term of explicit phonics teaching, Laura had learned to read.
The answer begins with a simple truth: speaking and reading are two fundamentally different things. We are born ready to speak, but not ready to read.

Unlike with spoken language, the brain didn’t evolve to read and write. Reading requires the brain to use existing systems that evolved for other purposes, getting them to work together in different ways.
We could give a child a bike but they’re highly unlikely to learn through exposure alone. They need to be taught. It’s just the same with reading.
Segmenting speech in this way is a significant obstacle in learning to read and spell because hearing individual speech sounds in words is not something we’re biologically programmed to do.

t: When Consistency Becomes Conformity
q: This is consistency of entitlement, and it matters enormously. But it is quite different from requiring every teacher to deliver that entitlement through the same lesson format, the same sequence of activities or the same routine at the same point in every lesson.

It is a concept from organisational theory that describes what happens when an organisation adopts the visible features associated with successful practice without necessarily developing the capability or understanding that made the original practice effective.

Teachers comply with the form while the function gradually disappears: retrieval questions are completed because it is the first five minutes, knowledge organisers are produced because they are expected, and lesson phases appear on slides because leaders look for them.
The things that are easiest to check can therefore become proxies for the things that matter most.

When practices are mistaken for principles, they become fixed. The question shifts from “Is this helping pupils learn what matters?” to “Is everyone doing it?” That is the point at which consistency starts to become conformity.
Perhaps the single most important diagnostic test is this: if the visible routine disappeared, what other evidence would tell us that the underlying principle was secure?
The aim is not identical practice. It is a shared commitment to strong principles, enacted intelligently.

t: The Leadership Knowledge That Complexity Demands
q: What matters in school improvement? Ultimately better outcomes for students. Upstream of this is improving teaching, and upstream of that is improving leadership.

When I switched from being the Headteacher of one school to another over a summer, the formal knowledge I possessed did not change. But my contextual knowledge dropped to almost zero over night, making me instantly less expert in my role as the Headteacher in the new school than I was the previous day for the old one.

But schools are complex systems, characterised by features such as emergence, unpredictability, self organisation and historical influence. In such conditions, knowledge of the specific system within which we work is vital.

However a leader can know their school intimately and still misjudge a decision, still miss what's actually driving their own reasoning, still fail to spot a pattern they've already lived through once before. Closing that gap takes something broader than local knowledge.

A leader with 20 years of experience might have done the job for that long without ever developing informal, impressionistic or self regulatory knowledge, repeating the same thought processes and decisions without evolution. Hidden knowledge can be built through experience but it is not a given that experience builds it.

t: Always Honor the Past Before Explaining What's Next
q: Amid change and transition, people go through an emotional stage of letting go of the old before they can commit to the new. Leaders who miss this essentially ask people to break ground on something new before they’ve finished with what came before.

t: What Self Respect Looks Like When Nobody Is Watching
q: Self respect is easy to talk about when life is visible. It is easy to keep your standards when people are watching, when your effort will be noticed, when your discipline has an audience, or when doing the right thing also makes you look like the kind of person you want others to admire.
Nobody knows whether you kept the promise you made to yourself that morning. Nobody sees whether you returned to the work after becoming distracted.

Nobody knows whether you told the whole truth when a smaller lie would have protected your image. Nobody sees the moment you could have taken an easier path without consequence and quietly chose not to.

These private decisions rarely feel important while they are happening. There is no applause attached to them. They do not immediately change your reputation, income, appearance, or position in life. Yet they slowly shape something beneath all of those things: whether you trust yourself.

t: We Owe Them More
q: The thing I remember-I will always remember it-was the eye contact. When adults saw each other, we stopped and looked each other full in the face. "How are you?" we asked.

The question was not really about being remembered. It was: Who are you responsible for? What are you doing with your time and energy that matters to someone besides yourself? Who has a claim on you? What do you owe?

I discovered how enormously difficult teaching is and how badly we prepare people to do it. Before long, I was writing again, this time about schools, curriculum, teaching, and what children need from the adults charged with educating them.

My colleague Yuval Levin has spent much of his career thinking and writing about the institutions of American life, and one of his most memorable insights is that institutions are not merely things that exist as platforms for our personal performance. At their best, they are molds that form us.

Police officers and other first responders ran toward people they did not know because those people were in their care. Duty was not an abstraction. It meant: Someone is depending on me, so I have to go.

t: Teaching on Purpose #15: Continuous and Enhanced Provision
q: Continuous provision refers to the carefully planned resources, materials and experiences that remain available for children to access independently throughout the day. Rather than rotating activities or relying solely on adult-directed tasks, practitioners organise the environment so that children repeatedly encounter opportunities to explore, apply and revisit important knowledge and skills.

Two years ago, Massachusetts voters eliminated the state's much-lauded MCAS test as a graduation requirement—much like the Board of Regents has done to New York's erstwhile exit exams—but the Bay State hasn't abandoned the concept of a consistent, externally validated measure of student learning.

Lest readers see New York's haziness as excusable, since full implementation won't occur until 2029, I'll observe that Massachusetts has until 2031. There's just no excuse for New York to be building the plane while flying it when 860,000 high schoolers' educations are at stake every year.

In sum, the aspirational nature of portraits of a graduate needn't come at the expense of substantive graduation requirements—the stuff that actually shapes instruction and learning. States adopting portraits would do well to be a Massachusetts, not a Monet.

When I shared this in a correspondence with my friend Jim, he said, "Diane McClain, one of my mentor teachers from Burlingame, just an amazing woman in her 70s now, said many times that we all need at least one person in our lives that we cannot stand the idea of disappointing.

And in his greater, much earlier days, Tiger Woods said he always imagined himself walking down the fairway every time with Arnold Palmer on one side and Jack Nicklaus on the other. It's a useful and demanding rubric of sorts.

The more I thought about it, the more I realized that Abby's wall wasn't just a funny thought — this spunky teenager walking out of her room, vowing not to disappoint the protagonist of Legally Blonde — but was in fact profound.
The responses were all over the place — some whimsical, some deep — and overall, it was probably my favorite writing warm-up prompt of the entire past school year.

t: Homeschooling Is More Normal Than You Think
q: Homeschooling in America today is "the site of a flourishing range of pedagogies, curricula, and experiments in education," reflecting the diversity of Americans.
Modern homeschooling is part of a long American tradition of parental involvement in children's education and community that began arguably with the Massachusetts School Laws of the 1640s.

The child is not the mere creature of the State," wrote Justice James McReynolds. And further: "The fundamental theory of liberty upon which all governments in this Union repose excludes any general power of the State to standardize its children by forcing them to accept instruction from public teachers only.

In a well-ordered society, children are not pitted against parents; men are not pitted against women; cities do not siphon resources from rural areas; and one's love of family, neighbor, culture, church, stranger, and nation are not in conflict.

They didn't send their children to district schools because they didn't want them to grow up with "the violent gang mind." But they would invite the neighbor kids—many from broken homes—over to their house after school hours to give them a safe haven and the experience of a loving home.

t: Help Your Middle Managers Be Better—Jellyfish?
q: But because your role entails lots of resolve and decisiveness, it's easy to treat everybody else's role as if that's what their work is like too. All they need, in other words, is directness and resoluteness.
Their role isn't just a smaller and less-empowered version of yours. Their role has its own indispensable way of standing within your organization.
But they don't just need competence in conveying information; they also need it for convincing people. And sometimes they themselves need convincing.

Following the example of deep canvassers like Dave Fleischer, you might coach your manager to ask, "On a scale of 1 to 10, how do you feel about the new policy?" That question gets their feelings out in the open, not so the manager can attack or avoid them, but so that skeptical employees can begin to query their own feelings.

If my higher-ups had been in my meeting, they might have simply counseled me to be more blunt, forceful, direct, terse. But that advice is roughly equivalent to telling a jellyfish to imitate a hammerhead.
They have complexly evolved identities that need your help to stay both firm and supple, flexible and strong, in the changeful conditions of leadership today.

t: Fathers and Sons 2: Your Depression Is Contagious, And Your Son Caught It
q: Even when he tries to conceal his emotional struggles, his children may still experience their effects. A father's anger can contribute to anger in his children. His depression can increase their risk of depression.

A meta-analysis of more than 7.1 million father-child pairs found that paternal depression was associated with a 42 percent greater risk of depression in children. When the father had a diagnosed depressive disorder, the risk was 65 percent higher.
Susan Schwartz calls a father's emotional struggles his "shadow." If a father does not confront his shadow, it can interfere with his ability to meet his son's needs and be a good father.

Boys need fathers who can embrace "the benefits of active participation in the lives of their sons." Left without this participation, a father may be physically present but emotionally withdrawn leaving the boy with father hunger.

Boys need fathers who can allow themselves to be "positive, loving, relating, nurturing, warm." Left without nurture fathers, sons experience a void in their fathers and learn to associate masculinity with emotional withholding.
Left withdrawn and disengaged the son may cry out for years for his father's love mixed with feelings of hurt, anger, disappointment and hope that dad will someday love him.

t: Dorothy Sayers: the Awake Mind as Author
q: Yet I would claim that Dorothy Sayers, like CS Lewis or Langston Hughes, can be read in a great texts program. The sum of the genius, the person behind the prose and poetry, is greater than any individual work.

This book is almost as close to Napoleon I as it is to us in time, but the novel does not feel dated to my college students. Sayers is both relying on Christian morality and on the creation of a genre, the detective novel, whose rules keep her prose (almost) timeless.
When she asks Are Women Human? or looks at the Lost Tools of Learning she also manages to stimulate a deeply conservative feminism and inspire the contemporary classical education program.
Sayers captures, however, a possibility that she lived: a deeply feminist traditionalism and a better vision for education than mere job training.

If Shakespeare had given us nothing greater than Henry VI (in all its uneven parts), then we might still read him to see the Bard of Avon who made a living, earned a title for his family, and yet also looked (fairly) deeply into the human condition. Dorothy Sayers is the equal of that Shakespeare.

t: AI Changes the Learner. But Do We Know How?
q: I was writing about a study in AI and Ethics that interviewed twenty-two professionals in healthcare and the military, people for whom a bad call is a catastrophe rather than an inconvenience. A screen puts a layer between you and the thing you are deciding about. The person becomes a percentage. The more often the machine is right, the less you argue with it.

Asking AI to argue with itself does not automatically protect human judgement. If the model supplies the answer, the objection, and the rebuttal, the learner can remain a spectator throughout an impressive simulation of critical thinking.

Twenty-two interviews can surface mechanisms that people recognise and describe. They cannot show that anyone's judgement durably changed. I called it evidence of a change when what I had was a well-described hypothesis about one.

On the 'learner as spectator' point, this is what I mean: a student can ask AI for an answer, ask it to challenge that answer, and then ask which argument is stronger. The transcript contains all the features we associate with critical thinking: claims, counterclaims, evidence, and revision, but they were generated by the model.

Give every student the same question. Have them fix their own position before any model sees it. That baseline does not have to be written: for some students writing is not the accessible route, and what matters is that the position exists and is recorded somehow, spoken, drawn or typed.

q: Students have had access to AI for their entire high school life. If we say nothing about AI we might assume that they won't use it, but it's likely that the burden of proof runs the other direction for our students.
We decided to make this a level 2 task, meaning AI could be used for finding sources and gathering data, but it could not be used for writing composition.
As I argued last week, one of the reasons students misuse AI is that they feel the task is beyond them. In order to support those who need it, we provided scaffolding for writing composition.

Another risk factor for AI misuse is a lack of visibility. Students can delay work, get to the last minute, panic, then outsource their task. To combat this, we set multiple checkpoints along the way.

I encourage my team to give one point of praise highlighting something that was done really well, and one specific fix that should be adopted in all future work. We've found this kind of feedback is the most actionable for the most students.

And that highlights a core truth about education in an AI world: while we need to make some changes, good teaching remains good teaching. AI has changed a number of things about education, but it's not as if we need to burn it all down and rebuild from the ashes.

t: A Word Of Caution: How Getting Promoted Quietly Turns Off Your Judgment
q: A manager corrects the report. A more senior colleague mentions that idea already failed back in 2019. A process catches the bad call before it ever reaches the client.

Then you move up. Promotion after promotion, climbing further into the corporate ladder. And the mesh keeps disappearing, one thread at a time, so slowly that nobody notices the exact moment it happened.
One day you walk out of a hard meeting and realize nobody pushed back on anything. From the top of your ego, that probably reads as a good sign. Alignment. Clarity. The team gets it.
Daniel Kahneman spent 500 pages mapping the systematic errors of human judgment in Thinking, Fast and Slow. We covered them last week.
It's far easier to spot someone else's mistake than your own. The observer isn't under pressure, has nothing riding on the outcome, doesn't need the story to sound good.
Not because your mind gets worse. Because the environment stops correcting you.
In a leadership seat, it doesn't happen on its own. It has to be built on purpose, against the incentive of nearly everyone around you.

t: A Leader's Guide to Waiting Well
q: David Maister's classic analysis of the psychology of waiting lines makes the case that distress in a queue has less to do with the clock than with how the wait is perceived.
But research on boredom and the brain's neural system suggests that idle, unstructured time is when the mind does some of its best creative work.
The counterintuitive idea is to occasionally let a wait be boring on purpose and to treat the discomfort as a signal that the mind is ready for the challenge of thinking privately.

Reflect and Confirm belong together, too. Reflecting means using your words to unlock their intended meaning. Confirming allows them to use their words to translate yours.

t: The Power No One Has to Give You
q: Murphy and his associates had studied 18,000 managers across 562 organizations and identified just over 1,000 people who demonstrated exceptional leadership ability. One of the findings was deceptively simple: people perceived as true leaders are those who value their own competence more than any externally bestowed affirmation.
Authority is conferred while leadership is developed and honed by people working to uplift others.
Leadership is not about men in suits. It is a way of life for those who know who they are and are willing to be their best to create the life they want to live.

Authority matters. We give people formal authority because societies and organizations need ways to make decisions, allocate resources, enforce laws, and hold responsibility. But authority is not the same as agency.
Agency is our voice. Our attention. Where we spend our money. What we are willing to question. Whom we invite into a conversation. What we create when what we need does not yet exist.

Control is inherently precarious. If my sense of power depends upon maintaining my title, keeping people aligned with me, accumulating more money, defeating an opponent, or ensuring that others behave as I wish, I am forever at risk of losing it.
This power is impossible for others to take without our consent. And it is what our current moment is asking us to reclaim.
It was never something another person could bestow upon us. It is ours to develop. And ours to choose.

t: Making the Audience the Hero in Your Presentations
q: In any presentation, the speaker is not the hero. The audience is. Presenters naturally feel they are the stars of the show since they're the ones on stage. But it is the audience that must adopt the ideas.
The presentation gets built around the audience's experience with the content, not the presenter's rationale, logic, or argument.

A leader announcing a reorganization, for example, doesn't open with the reasons behind the shuffle. They open with the tension the team members feel, such as uncertainty, capacity, and trepidation about what it means for them.
Instead, they arrive with one clear and useful gift, an insight, a framework, a solution, and hand it over to the audience almost immediately.
A good presentation then alternates between what is (the status quo) and what could be (the vision of something better). Duarte calls this shape the Sparkline
This alternating structure is what keeps the tension alive long enough for the audience to feel the stakes, rather than simply being told about them.
When the presenter steps back and hands the audience the pen, the story becomes theirs to finish. The presenter simply points the way.

t: Interview with Jerry Crisci: AI Is Changing the World. Who's Redesigning School? September 8, 2026
q: If you're going to be running any kind of innovation in your organization, the bottom line is: do people in your organization have the permission to experiment and do things that would be truly innovative

If you're going to be running any kind of innovation in your organization, the bottom line is: do people in your organization have the permission to experiment and do things that would be truly innovative? Our superintendent wisely said, when we founded our center, that technology was the fulcrum, not the focus.

The difference with AI, I would say, is that it has three components that the rest of technology didn't have: speed, or acceleration, we've never seen a technology be this quickly adopted and this fast-moving; lenses, people looking at this technology through all different lenses, with AI everyone has different viewpoints; and ownership, with technology it was pretty clear who owned the learning, teachers were in control of things, with AI we don't have ownership clearly defined.

I realized that teachers were doing a great job of redesigning their curriculum and instruction with schools as they currently are and with AI as they currently were, and I said this is not going to continue down this path, I really need to make people more aware of what the future of school could be.

There's a bill in New York, the FOCUS Act, that wants to ban all internet-connected devices in grades kindergarten through fifth grade. We had all of our fifth graders in Scarsdale do an independent research project, and they had to do internet research. What do you do if they have no technology?

I use an AI simulator. I show them how it constructs a sentence word by word. I also show them that it's not really thinking. It's pattern matching. I think that is so important, not just for teachers to understand, but when you hear about students engaging in relationships with AI, thinking of that as a person. Here's what's happening behind the scenes, it simulates that you're talking to a person, but in fact you're talking to a broken calculator.
There should be a national initiative that really creates almost a series of lab schools and a dedicated research institution to focus on AI and education.

t: Death by a Thousand Caveats
q: There's nothing wrong with identifying limitations in research. The problem is when this becomes death by a thousand caveats: finding enough reasons that individual pieces of evidence don't apply until we're left with no evidence at all.

A decision is informed by the evidence, interpreted through professional expertise and adapted to the context in which it is being applied.

To understand whether explicit instruction is effective across different contexts, AERO conducted a review of more than 328 studies. The review found that explicit instruction is an effective teaching practice across a variety of contexts and for different subgroups of students.

t: Would They Still Choose You?
q: Trust is different because it carries a further vulnerability: when a person lets us down, the natural response is not just disappointment but a feeling of betrayal.

Harvard Business Review has argued that the quest to be absolutely necessary is often limiting rather than protective. Because the very thing that makes you hard to remove can also make you hard to promote.

So being needed feels safer in the moment mainly for one reason: the other person cannot walk away from you. But a position that depends on someone having no choice is not loyalty, and it is not strength. It is just the absence of an exit.

There is a single counterfactual that cuts straight through this: if this person suddenly had a genuinely good alternative to you, would they still come to you, or would they take it? Trust survives that question. Need fails it.

That kind of work does not grade itself. There is no test suite for materiality. There is no clean answer key for professional judgment under uncertainty.
The question that best indicates which jobs will be affected most is: How quickly and objectively can we tell whether the work was done well?

We should take technologists' warnings seriously while recognizing that their experience with code is not a complete theory of the future of work.

t: The Hidden Cost of Thinking You Know Someone
q: What we believe affects what we notice about someone. Our brains can only consciously process a tiny fraction of the information around us at any moment.

There's a good chance it's the comment that fits what you already believe about her. This is a type of confirmation bias: we see whatever confirms our initial assumption about a person, while tending to miss evidence that points the other way.

If you already think of him as highly capable, you might see the question as evidence of good judgment: he knows when it's worth getting another perspective. But if you've begun to doubt his capabilities, exactly the same question might strike you as further evidence that he lacks independence.

Over time, small daily differences can compound and create very different paths for a person. One path might lead to micromanagement, low motivation, and slowed development; the other might build toward opportunities for growth, advancement, and agency.
When we notice we've become very sure in our beliefs about someone, it's often worth creating room to check for other interpretations.
The point is to hold these beliefs lightly enough that you can still recognize the signs pointing in another direction, toward a bigger set of possibilities for this person you care about.

t: All Call: What Are You Woodenizing Right Now?
q: Woodenization is first and foremost an attitude that says, I assume that if I want my students to do something well, it's my job to be clear about how to do it.
The name comes from Coach John Wooden, who famously taught his collegiate athletes how to put on their socks and tie their shoes on the first day of practice each season.
When Woodenizing, teachers are wise to think in terms of two categories: Smallies, stuff that can be taught once, with total clarity, and then reinforced thereafter. Smallies are matters of habit.
Biggies, stuff that needs to be taught multiple times over a time period in order for students to better understand how to do it well. Biggies are matters of skill.

The key question of the Woodenizer is: what learning-conducive behaviors would I like all of my students to master? From there, pick a few smallies and one biggie that you most want your students to master, and start breaking them down with as much clarity and simplicity and power as you can.

t: The Duty of Memory
q: This discovery of yours will create forgetfulness in the learners' souls, because they will not use their memories; they will trust to the external written characters and not remember of themselves.

The specific which you have discovered is an aid not to memory, but to reminiscence, and you give your disciples not truth, but only the semblance of truth; they will be hearers of many things and will have learned nothing; they will appear to be omniscient and will generally know nothing; they will be tiresome company, having the show of wisdom without the reality.

The person with a vast library, in one sense, has much knowledge available to him, but he does not himself know anything unless he takes it upon himself to inscribe that knowledge not only in books but on his own soul.

What your average person knows today often doesn't rival what a sixth grader knew in the 1940's. We rely on something else, something external, to contain the knowledge for us and we are content to look it up only if and when it becomes relevant and, in most cases, we release that information back into the void about 15 seconds later.

Knowledge is a prerequisite for wisdom and wisdom is a prerequisite for prudence and prudence is knowing what is right and true, understanding what one ought to do in light of that knowledge, and then actually doing it when the time for action comes.

Socrates' point is well made because the fool of his day would treat books like the fool of our day treats ChatGPT, an excuse not to know, not to be made better by effort and intentional engagement in learning.

t: The 3 Reasons Smart Leaders Produce Weak Strategies
q: Even an MBA teaches you ABOUT strategy. It never has you build one.

SWOT, Porter, Blue Ocean: everyone applies the same tools to the same market. Filling in a canvas feels like progress, but no framework makes the hard choices for you. So the framework produces a document, and the real questions stay open.

Goals for every department, so nobody feels left out. “Growth,” “efficiency” and “innovation” all at once, with no choice between them. Nothing the company decided NOT to do. A plan everyone approves because it commits nobody.

You take last year’s document, or a template from your previous company. You update the numbers, refresh the market slide, add the current buzzwords. You fill every box: mission, SWOT, pillars, initiatives, KPIs. The deck looks complete, so leadership approves it. Six months later, nothing has changed in how the company operates.
Here’s a quick test. Take your current strategy document and ask: “Could a competitor paste their logo on this deck and change almost nothing?” If yes, you have a template, not a strategy.

To start with the first critique - the idea that there are no papers on science and literacy integration that use standardized assessments is the most egregious. Twenty of the thirty-three studies in this collection use standardized assessments.

In the Romance and Vitale series, upper elementary students received two hours a day of integrated science and literacy content. This is contrasted with control groups who received an hour and a half a day of similar literacy intervention plus a half hour of non-integrated science instruction. They consistently found that the treatment group outperformed the control (1992, 2001), and even found that the effects lasted into middle school (2011).

In over thirty studies on this topic, many with multiple measures of comprehension, there is only one singular significant negative effect. This effect was seen in second graders in a three day study where baseline pretests were not given.

t: Can We Settle for Assimilation?

Having restricted growth to increasing one's knowledge, it then flattens knowledge to mean only technical information; the assimilation of new data; the storing of facts -- all things nonfiction works are generally designed to help us do.

The Philosopher Peter Kreeft suggests that the human soul has three prophets: the intellect, the imagination, and the conscience. These prophets reveal to us three aspects of reality: truth, beauty, and goodness, respectively. Nonfiction generally appeals only, or at least primarily, to the first of these: to propositional truths, understood as external facts.

One of the reasons fiction is indispensable to the serious reader is that it makes up a substantial part of the culture-expressing and culture-shaping body of literature. Works of fiction are a gateway into understanding culture -- whether that of others, or your own.

Speaking in great generality, nonfiction is adept at filling and forming the head (the rational; the intellectual), while fiction is adept at forming the chest (the sentiments, the orientation, the conviction). If we wish to avoid men without chests or bodies without heads, it's a good idea to include both fiction and nonfiction in our diet.

People wonder why the novel is the most popular form of literature; people wonder why it is read more than books of science or books of metaphysics. The reason is very simple; it is merely that the novel is more true than they are.
Fiction stands as something of a bulwark against this trend by preserving that wholeness and presenting it to us in a complete story. And stories are powerful -- they move us and help us remember.

t: The Single Point of Failure
q: The habit is finding the single point of failure. Every company I diligence has one. Sometimes the founder knows it and is hoping I won't ask and sometimes they genuinely don't see it, which is worse, honestly, because you can't fix what you can't name.

Nobody sets out to build a single point of failure. It gets built by accident, by rewarding what's working today and never asking the boring question of what happens if the one load-bearing thing doesn't show up tomorrow.

Broadly: portfolios under ten positions tend to return well under invested capital, and portfolios of twelve or more, held over five years plus, do meaningfully better and more reliably. That gap isn't stock-picking talent. It's whether you built something with more than one leg under it.

I built a household on one leg and didn't notice, for the same reason the undocumented codebase works fine until the one person who understands it takes a week off. My husband ran things I never learned to run.

If your company depends on the knowledge in one person's head, or one customer's renewal decision, or one investor's name standing in for diligence you never ran yourself, that isn't traction or conviction either but a single point of failure with a nicer outfit on.
The companies I got a reputation for reading correctly were never the ones hiding something from me. I was the one hiding it. From myself, mostly.

t: The People Closest to the Problem Already Know the Answer
q: When Kaya became Chancellor of DC Public Schools, she inherited a district in a free fall — the lowest-performing urban school district in the United States, 40 consecutive years of enrollment decline, a graduation rate under 50%, and 29 data systems that didn't talk to each other.

Kaya's core move was refusing to treat her constituents like children. When schools had to close, she didn't hand the community a decision — she handed them a proposal and then put her team's data next to the community's data.
Her point: people are reasonable. We act like they're crazy, but they're only "crazy" because we don't give them the information.

In order to give her changes their best shot at becoming permanent, Kaya built a five-point plan simple enough that anyone in the district could recite it, because memorability is how change survives past the leader who started it.
He asked, "So why would you do it that way? Why wouldn't you just do it the Kaya Henderson way?" Kaya refers to this as the most liberating thing anyone ever said to her.
Kaya led by her own hallmarks, which, in her words, are love, authenticity, believing the best about people, and co-creation.

t: The Most Dangerous Moment in Any Decision Is the Moment You Feel Sure (leadwithkelly.substack.com), September 1, 2026
q: A man knocked on my door in San Francisco and handed me legal papers. I was being sued for the people I had just hired. The ink on their offers was barely dry.

There was a problem I could see clearly. The company was full of brilliant software people and almost no one who understood the machines. You cannot predict when a machine will fail if no one in the building knows how it works.
So I was about to hand the best mechanical engineers in the world to a company that believed mechanical engineers were a thing of the past. Two tribes. Each was certain the other was beneath them.

The people were everything I said they were. It was beside the point. The outcome was never going to be decided by talent. It was going to be decided by a culture I had watched reject the idea of them before they ever arrived.
That is the trap. Certainty about the one thing you can measure becomes certainty about the things you cannot. Will the market show? Will the cultures merge? Can I hold this together on will alone?
Now, when a decision gives off that clean, confident hum, the part that says, "At least this choice I know for sure," I have learned to treat it as the warning, not the green light.

t: The Leader You're Looking For Is Hiding in Plain Sight
q: I also began to understand something I hadn’t anticipated: holding a position of authority did not necessarily mean someone was leading. People with enormous institutional power could become consumed with preserving that power, navigating the next election, protecting a department, defending an old decision, managing competing interests or simply keeping a system moving.

Again and again, leadership often appeared in places where no one had bestowed the title: a colleague speaking up in a meeting; a junior member going on the record when senior members would not; a neighbor organizing and advocating for a change everyone knew was needed; one person willing to have the conversation everyone else had been avoiding.

America cannot afford to make leadership the responsibility of a relatively small group of people. There are more than 340 million of us. Imagine the capacity we leave untouched when most of us assume leadership belongs primarily to someone else.

As John Lewis reminded us, “You must be bold, brave, and courageous and find a way… to get in the way.” Leadership is present whenever we recognize that what we do can affect what happens next, and decide to act accordingly.

My high school civics teacher probably had no idea what would follow from his suggestion that I spend my afternoons working for a local state legislator. He didn’t need to know. He saw something, cared enough to act and created an opening for me to discover what I could do.

t: The Era of Cognitive Automation (fivetwelvethirteen.substack.com), September 1, 2026
q: For the entirety of the 20th century, across the developed world, each generation of humans was a bit smarter than the last. The best evidence we have for this is the Flynn effect. Humans have steadily improved on IQ tests over that century, where each decade the average test-taker improved by about 3 points.
We can’t attribute much of these gains to what was happening in schools. There’s just no evidence that the quality of education has made a substantive difference.
Either there was a broad conspiracy across almost the entire developed world to ruin schools while also somehow making adults decades out of school dumber, or the cause isn’t actually in schools.

Here’s the story I’m telling. For a long time, as the world became more complex, that complexity caused humans to think harder and think more and made us smarter. Then, a second trend began: cognitive automation displaced some of that thinking, slowly at first but then faster and faster.
I’m not saying school is useless. If school disappeared tomorrow, student achievement would plummet. Covid was an unfortunate but illustrative natural experiment to prove that point.
Horace complained over two thousand years ago about kids these days, and we haven’t stopped since. Every generation has argued that we are declining from some golden age in the past.
We won’t build a better education system by looking to the past. It will be something built, brick by brick, by humble, knowledgeable, passionate, and persistent educators.

t: Sisyphus Versus the Flywheel September 1, 2026
q: In the Sisyphus Model, a city's schools get so bad that the mayor or the state takes over. They appoint some brave new leader who has the authority to concentrate decision-making power, adopt new systems, and bring in new people. With luck, they can push student achievement up the metaphorical hill.

Celebrations ensue, and the hard-charging leader steps out of the picture. But over time, the political winds change, the new systems weaken, old habits return, and the rock starts rolling back down the hill.

Under the Flywheel Model there is no one hero. Instead of centralizing power under a single entity or person, a city devolves much of its decision-making authority to individual schools and school networks.

City leaders measure results, let successful schools grow, and close schools that consistently fail to attract families or produce results. With luck, successful schools grow and replicate, new schools learn from what works, and the lowest-performing and most under-enrolled schools close.

As I describe these models, I have real-world examples in mind. Both models have good stories to tell and have produced genuine successes. But which one would you bet on to make the most progress over time?

q: Starting as an ECT in primary is a daunting feeling. Suddenly, you go from being a student teacher in someone else's class to having your own class.

As an ECT, you should not have been given a class with particular behavioural issues (and if you find out that you have been, this is a huge red flag about the school). However, any class in a mainstream primary school will have its issues.

It's best to be really firm on rules and routines at the outset when the children are sussing you out and considering whether to push the line. It's quite easy to relax a little later on if you have been too insistent on something.

I am a strong believer that behaviour should be regarded as part of the curriculum and needs to be taught just like everything else. In particular, good behaviour in school involves a whole set of individual behaviours which need to be taught.

By the end of the first week, some of your more enterprising students will be testing boundaries. It's important to reinforce them at this point because it will only get harder in weeks 2, 3 and thereafter.

This is a recipe for burnout and, in my opinion, a nonsensical way to run a school. Primary schools vary hugely in the amount of shared resources they have and their attitude to using them so you will need to scope this out quickly.
The basic idea is simple. You tell children how you want them to participate before telling them what you want them to do.

t: Experts Shape Meaning (admiredleadership.substack.com), September 1, 2026
q: The last word doesn't refer to holding the floor last or making the last point. Nor does it mean advocating last or even speaking before the discussion ends.

For a true expert, having the last word means being the one whose framing survives the discussion. It means that when the conversation is over and people depart, the frame they carry with them is the expert's interpretation.
The discipline is taking the complex and noisy and making it simple and clean. Done poorly, it is a crude oversimplification. Done smartly, it adds an instant clarity to the room.

A room full of people can spend an hour debating a topic, but a true expert closes the exchange by saying, in effect, "Here is what actually matters." That statement is what persists as the rest fades away.

Experts often signal that an issue is settled, describing the terrain so clearly that further arguments feel unnecessary. An expert has failed if they let a discussion trail off into ambiguity or let someone else plant the frame.
The right to define what just happened isn't handed to anyone. Experts earn it, one accurate frame at a time.

q: What we tell ourselves matters. Our internal conversations influence how we feel, how we behave, how we communicate, and ultimately what happens next.
After you pause and separate the facts from the story, the next step is to notice the story itself. What are you telling yourself about the situation?
In leadership, our internal narratives can have a tremendous impact. We may tell ourselves someone does not respect us, a team member should know better, a mistake is unacceptable.
Once we can see the story we are telling ourselves, we have more choice about whether we want to keep carrying it forward. That is personal empowerment.

You cannot always control what happens before the pause. You cannot control how another person chooses to behave. But you can become more intentional about the story you carry forward and the person you choose to be within it.

t: Being Available Is How I Lost A Year (summermulder.substack.com), September 1, 2026
q: I never finished the Skool community. We ran it free for our clients, extra support on top of what they were already paying for. I'd launched it with a few modules and about a hundred members had joined.

It sat on my list for over a year, sliding forward one square at a time, and I don't think there was ever a single day where I looked at it and decided not to do it. It just kept losing to whatever was in front of me.

I think about it more than the failures that cost money, because it's such clean evidence of a pattern that ran my entire working life. The thing only I could and should do got pushed. Every single time.

There was something else underneath it too, and it took me a long time to see. I wanted my team to know I cared as much as they did. If they had an idea for an email campaign, I wrote it that same day.

t: Back to School: We Are All Teachers of Language September 1, 2026
q: We all teach language, sometimes explicitly and analytically, always implicitly and informally. For all formal education is conducted in and through words, through language.

Our language is not just a means of “content delivery”—it is always a co-subject, the background and scenery, the substrate, the foundation upon which the structure of the arts and sciences is built, even as other academic and intellectual and moral and aesthetic topics appear to be the sole concern.

t: AI in Education #13: Five Things I Learned from Joe Liemandt about Motivation, Data, and the Future of the Teaching Profession
q: His reasoning is about motivation, which Joe reckons explains 90% of Alpha's success. He points to Laurence Holt's 5% problem: the finding that many EdTech products' positive results are only positive when you exclude 95% of the students who fail to engage with the product.
